roots.name: Mainboard passive components
roots.description: The roughly 250-odd resistors, capacitors, trimmers and networks soldered to a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 motherboard. No ICs, no connectors: only the two-terminal and adjustable parts that set the bias, timing and filtering of everything else on the board.
roots.note: Population figures are taken from a transcription of the 250407 bill of materials; Commodore shipped several board revisions (250407, 250425, 250466, 250469) and the exact mix of disc vs monolithic ceramic capacitors moved between them.

facts.label: Trimmers
facts.value: 1 x 500 ohm trimmer potentiometer (R27), 1 x variable capacitor

children.name: Resistors
children.description: Fixed resistors on the 250407: about seventy 1/4 W axial parts in values from 100 ohm to 1 megohm, plus four thick-film SIP resistor networks and one 500 ohm trimmer. Almost all were 5 percent carbon film; the handful of 1 percent metal film parts sat in the VIC-II colour and timing network.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: axial, 6.3 x 2.3 mm, 0.63 mm lead pitch

children.name: Discrete axial resistor families
children.description: Three manufacturing routes to a 1/4 W axial resistor coexisted in 1982. The 250407 used overwhelmingly carbon film; carbon composition was still common in cheaper consumer goods; metal film was reserved for precision.

children.name: Carbon film resistor (1/4 W axial)
children.description: The bulk of the board's resistors. A thin, discontinuous film of carbon and clay laid on a hollow alumina ceramic tube; carbon loading sets the resistance. Cheap, 5 percent, and tolerant of being bent during manual insertion.

facts.label: Resistance
facts.value: 1 ohm to 10 Mohm, here 100 ohm to 1 Mohm

children.name: Ceramic tube substrate
children.description: A thin-wall extruded alumina tube, 0.5 mm outside diameter, whose wall carries the film. Hollow construction halves the ceramic mass per resistor, and the tube's inner bore is what the trimmer's abrasive cut reaches.
children.note: The Bayer refinery that turns bauxite into this alumina, and its caustic-soda digestion, are metal.alumina and metal.bayer. An earlier local copy of that chain named potassium hydroxide as the 1982 digestant, which is wrong: caustic soda was the mainstream digestant.

children.name: Moulded epoxy body
children.description: The trimmed resistor is transfer-moulded in epoxy, or coated in a phenolic shell, sealing the film from humidity. Moulding compound is a phenolic or epoxy resin filled with silica flour.
children.note: Not established: transfer moulding in epoxy versus a phenolic shell coating for these bodies, the humidity-seal purpose, and silica-flour filler in the moulding compound.

children.name: Carbon composition resistor
children.description: A rod of carbon and clay, compression-moulded into a small cylinder with metal end caps. Very cheap and very noisy, with a wide temperature coefficient and drift. Still used in 1982 in low-cost consumer goods and audio gear, but on the C64 itself it was already being displaced by carbon film.
children.note: Some very early Commodore boards (VIC-20, early PET) did use composition resistors; the 250407 does not appear to.

children.name: Swaged metal end caps and wire leads
children.description: Soft tin or brass caps are pressed over the moulded slug, then a tinned copper wire lead is swaged inside the cap, giving the familiar bulbous ends of a composition resistor.
children.note: Lead wire is tin-plated copper drawn from rod, not tinned after the fact.

facts.label: End cap material
facts.value: tin or brass, soft enough to swage

facts.label: End cap ore
facts.value: cassiterite SnO2, 0.1-1 % SnO2 in alluvial workings

children.name: Metal film resistor (1 % precision)
children.description: A NiCr or FeCr film vacuum-deposited onto an alumina substrate, then laser-trimmed to a tight tolerance. Where the VIC-II colour burst and the composite video level had to be set to a few parts in a thousand, a 1 percent metal film part was used instead of a 5 percent carbon film.
children.note: The 250407's parts list is dominated by 5 percent parts; which individual reference designators were 1 percent metal film is not confirmed.

children.name: Flat ceramic substrate (not a tube)
children.description: Metal film parts use a flat alumina bar or a flat ceramic tube rather than a tube-with-a-skin, because the uniform flat substrate is what makes laser scribing produce a stable, precise spiral.
children.note: Not established: that metal film parts use a flat alumina bar or flat ceramic tube rather than a tube-with-a-skin, and the causal link to stable laser scribing. No source consulted describes axial metal film substrates.

children.name: Termination cap and lead
children.description: A crimped steel or aluminium cap grips the lead and makes contact with the film, then the whole assembly is plated in nickel. Metal film parts are always nickel-plated leads, never bare tin.
children.note: Not established: the crimped steel or aluminium cap, the nickel plating, or the claim that metal film parts are always nickel-plated and never bare tin. No document consulted describes axial metal film terminations.

children.name: Wirewound power resistor
children.description: Resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin and vitreously enamelled. Used for the few watts-and-above duties - notably the 7805 regulator's dropping resistor and the video level network. Accurate, stable, but large and inductive.
children.note: Wound resistors do not appear in the 250407 BOM I checked; included because they were the standard answer for the same problems in the C64's power supply and peripherals of the same era.

children.name: Ceramic bobbin
children.description: A grooved steatite or alumina former on which a length of enamelled resistance alloy wire is wound. Steatite (magnesium silicate) was the classic low-cost bobbin material.
children.note: Not established: a grooved steatite versus alumina former wound with enamelled resistance alloy wire, and steatite as the classic low-cost bobbin material for the board's wirewounds.

children.name: Metal-foil precision resistor
children.description: An ultra-precise resistor built from rolled, etched metal foil - nickel, a nickel-chromium-iron alloy, or copper - clamped between a rigid steel/ceramic case and a polished die. Changing the roll geometry stretches the foil, so the resistance can be set with a screw to one part in a million.
children.note: Included to explain the 'foil' end of the precision-resistor family. No metal-foil parts appear in a Commodore 64; these were calibration standards in the lab and appeared in later high-precision analogue equipment.

Not established: three coexisting 1-4 W axial manufacturing routes in 1982, and the 250407 split of overwhelmingly carbon film with carbon composition still common elsewhere and metal film reserved for precision.

children.name: Thick-film cermet SIP resistor networks
children.description: The four resistor arrays on the 250407: two 8-way isolated 33 ohm packs (series terminators on the DRAM data bus), one 8-way 3k3 bussed pack and one 10-way 3k3 bussed pack. Each is one alumina substrate with several ruthenium-oxide resistive tracks screen-printed and fired together.
children.note: A RIFA 481 resistor pack is sometimes quoted for this position. RIFA (British Insulated Callender's Cables, Boxhill, UK) did supply SIP resistor networks to the European electronics trade in the 1980s, but no direct evidence has been found that a RIFA 481 is fitted to a C64 mainboard - treat that specific part number as unverified. A Bourns 4308R-series or equivalent Vishay pack is the functionally correct part.

facts.label: Arrays on board
facts.value: 4 (RP1, RP2 = 33 ohm isolated 8-way; RP3 = 3k3 bussed 8-way; RP4 = 3k3 bussed 10-way)

children.name: Alumina substrate with printed elements
children.description: A 0.6 mm thick 96 percent alumina bar, pre-fired and metallised. Conductive paste is printed through a photo-plated stainless screen onto the top face only, then the whole bar is fired to fuse the glass frit and mature the resistor.
children.note: Not established: 0.6 mm thick 96 percent alumina bar pre-fired and metallised for these networks, 2.54 mm print pitch, and photo-plated stainless screen printing on the top face only followed by glass-frit firing.

children.name: Trim and adjustable resistors
children.description: The single adjustable part on the 250407 is R27, a 500 ohm cermet trimmer potentiometer that biases U31's crystal oscillator so the 14.31818 MHz colour subcarrier lands exactly on NTSC's subcarrier frequency. It is the reason a C64 needs no colour adjustment in normal use but will show colour shimmer when the crystal ages.
children.note: On later C64 boards (the '8710' revision and Commodore's own C64C), this variable resistor was replaced with a trimmer capacitor in the crystal's load network. Both do the same job: pulling the oscillator to exactly the right frequency.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: +/-10 % body; the ADJUSTMENT is what matters

children.name: Cermet resistive element and track
children.description: A thick-film RuO2 resistive track deposited on the top face of an alumina substrate, with a metal-foil wiper that slides along it. Because the element is a printed film rather than a carbon blob, the tracking is smooth and the part does not develop a scratchy potentiometer feel the way a carbon composition pot does. The usable travel is a fraction of the physical length, because the track is designed to put most of its resistance in the middle of the sweep - that is how a 500 ohm trimmer gets a usable 0-500 ohm range out of a single turn of the adjuster screw.

facts.label: Wiper
facts.value: Ni alloy or precious metal, fork or blade

children.note: That a cermet - a ceramic/metal mixture - is a standard potentiometer resistive element is documented, as is ruthenium oxide among the cermet conductors. Not established: the 100 ohm to 1 Mohm per square sheet-resistance range, the specific wiper alloys, and the design intent of concentrating most of the resistance in the middle of the sweep.

children.name: Adjuster screw and slider
children.description: A knurled brass or stainless screw drives a moulded slider that rides the wiper along the track. Backing-off epoxy locks the setting once the board is aligned.

children.name: Adjuster screw
children.description: A brass or stainless screw, knurled or slotted, driving the slider. Brass is the usual choice because it machines cleanly at small diameters and does not gall against the moulded slider.
children.note: Not established: brass or stainless, knurled or slotted, and the anti-galling argument against a moulded slider. Multiturn trimmers use a lead screw and are documented; the material of this adjuster screw is not.
Not established: knurled brass versus stainless screw, a moulded slider riding the wiper along the track, and backing-off epoxy locking the setting after board alignment.

Not established: about seventy 1-4 W axial parts with the listed values, four thick-film SIP networks plus one 500 ohm trimmer, the 6.3 x 2.3 mm axial package, and the almost-all-5-percent-carbon-film with a few 1-percent-metal-film parts in the VIC-II colour and timing network.

children.name: Monolithic ceramic capacitor (MLCC)
children.description: The 0.1 uF bypass and small timing capacitors. Dozens of layers of barium-titanate ceramic with screen-printed metal electrodes buried between them, then fired and terminated. Monolithic construction gives huge capacitance in a tiny body because the electrode area is the whole face of every layer.
children.note: The 250407 parts list as transcribed by the replica-board project specifies 0.1 uF 50 V X7R, 0.22 uF Z5U and small C0G parts; Commodore's exact mix of ceramic disc versus monolithic changed between board revisions, and the X7R/Z5U designations are modern restatements of what were then simply 'ceramic'.

facts.label: Dielectric classes
facts.value: X7R / Z5U for the big values, C0G for the small timing caps

facts.label: Size (1982)
facts.value: ~2.5 x 3.2 mm radial blocks and discs

children.name: Aluminium electrolytic capacitor
children.description: The polarised bulk capacitors: about fifteen 10 uF/25 V radial parts decoupling the SID and video analogue rails, plus larger axial 100-2200 uF parts on the rectified supply rails. Value comes from a nanometres-thick anodic oxide on etched aluminium foil soaked in electrolyte - cheap, large capacitance, and the bulk of the board's supply-rail filtering.

facts.label: Radial parts
facts.value: ~15 x 10 uF/25 V, 5 x 5 mm can

children.name: High-purity anode foil, rolled and etched
children.description: High-purity aluminium foil, roughened by electrochemical etching so that the surface becomes a mass of microscopic pits, then anodically formed to grow an insulating alumina layer on it. Etching multiplies the effective area of the anode, which is how a hundred microfarads fits into a 5 mm can. The foil is wound with a separate cathode foil and absorbent separator, and the liquid electrolyte is the actual second electrode.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: hot HCl/HNO3, or a sodium chlorate bath

facts.label: Surface area gain
facts.value: up to about x200 relative to a smooth surface, depending on the rated voltage

children.note: Not established, and contradicted by the standard construction description: the anode foil is quoted as at least 99.99 % pure aluminium and 20-100 um thick, and etching as giving a surface-area increase of up to a factor of 200. The 99.5-99.7 % purity, 12-25 um thickness and x50-x100 area gain quoted here are not supported by any source consulted, and the etch multiplies the anode area, not the cathode's.

children.name: Cathode foil
children.description: Aluminium foil, usually a cheaper alloy and often unetched, serving as the return electrode. It carries no dielectric of its own; its job is simply to collect the return current through the electrolyte.

children.name: Tantalum capacitor
children.description: A polarised capacitor built around sintered tantalum powder with an anodic oxide dielectric and a solid electrolyte. Low leakage and very good stability for its size; in the early 1980s tantalum was the default decoupling choice on high-performance professional digital boards.
children.note: The breadbin C64 250407 uses aluminium electrolytics and ceramics, NOT tantalum on its logic. Tantalum was standard in the same period's professional and instrumentation designs and appears elsewhere in Commodore hardware of the era. Included for era breadth and for the tantalum supply story; do not read it as mainboard content.

children.name: Sintered tantalum anode
children.description: Capacitor-grade tantalum powder is pressed around a tantalum riser wire that becomes the anode connection, and the pellet is vacuum sintered at high temperature so that the powder takes on a sponge-like structure with all particles interconnected. The Ta2O5 dielectric then grows on that internal surface, which is why a gram of powder stores far more capacitance than a gram of film.

facts.label: Powder
facts.value: typical particle size 2-10 um; finer grades give higher surface area per unit volume

facts.label: CV product
facts.value: about 20,000 uF.C/V per gram for the earlier material; the roughly ten-fold rise to 200,000 is described as a later achievement and so cannot be attributed to 1982

children.note: Contradicted on the powder figure: capacitor-grade tantalum powder is described as having a typical particle size of 2-10 um, not sub-micron, and the quoted CV/g range of 20k-200k is stated as a ten-fold improvement achieved since the mid-1980s, so 100k-200k uF.C/V per gram cannot be attributed to 1982. The sinter figure is also given as 1200-1800 C, wider than the 1200-1400 C here. The 2-4 m2/g surface area is unsourced.

children.name: Early-1980s tantalum supply squeeze
children.description: Capacitor tantalum depends on columbite-tantalite ore, essentially all of it from the Kivu region of Zaire and neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi. A collapse in the electronics market in 1982-83 drained the supply chain's stocks, then demand spiked again in 1984 on the PC and automotive booms. The USGS records a significant spike in tantalum demand in 1984, with US factory sales of tantalum capacitors at an all-time high and escalating prices pushing consumers to substitute aluminium parts and to design tantalum out where they could. It was a real, documented shortage in exactly the C64's production window. The documented engineering response was to reduce tantalum content where possible, substitute aluminium electrolytics, and lengthen qualified lead times - a good example of how a metals shortage propagates into board design decisions within eighteen months.
children.note: The 1984 demand spike and the all-time-high factory-sales figure are verified against USGS Circular OF01-349. No peak capacitor-grade powder price for 1983-84 is stated here because no reliable figure for that grade and year could be sourced. The recycling loop is a real node under the capacitor; this note carries the shortage itself.

children.name: Ceramic disc (monolithic disc) capacitor
children.description: A single fired barium-titanate disc with silver electrodes fired onto its two faces. Enormous capacitance for its size and very cheap, but microphonically noisy, temperature-drifty and physically large, with no self-cancelling inductance. On C64 boards of this era the small 0.1 uF parts were already largely the multilayer form.

facts.label: Electrodes
facts.value: silver paste screen-printed and fired on

facts.label: Breakdown
facts.value: ~2.5 kV per um of effective dielectric thickness (design guideline)

facts.label: Weakness
facts.value: resonant above a few MHz; large body

children.note: Not established: silver paste screen-printed and fired as the electrodes on these discs, the 0.1 uF 50 V value, the 2.5 kV per um design guideline, resonance above a few MHz, and that the small 0.1 uF parts were already largely multilayer on C64 boards of this era.

children.name: Film capacitors (polyester / polystyrene)
children.description: Film capacitors use a thin metallised plastic film as the dielectric. Non-polar, stable, and tolerant of voltage and temperature excursions. The C64 uses polyester (Melinex/PET) for coupling and decoupling in the analogue paths; polystyrene appears in the precision timing networks of the same era's equipment.

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: vacuum-deposited aluminium or zinc on the film

children.name: Polystyrene film capacitor
children.description: A polystyrene dielectric: exceptionally stable, very low dielectric absorption and low loss, historically the timing capacitor of choice for precision RC oscillators before polystyrene's poor mechanical behaviour pushed it into disfavour. Used in analogue equipment of the era, but not a significant part on the C64 mainboard.
children.note: Polystyrene parts are not confirmed in the 250407 parts list.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: polystyrene, very low loss, very stable

children.note: Construction and era are documented: metallised aluminium or zinc deposited directly on the plastic film or a separate metal foil; paper and metallised paper almost completely replaced by PET film for low-power DC applications from around 1980; polystyrene used where its near-zero temperature coefficient suits tuned circuits. The board value is now confirmed from the primary parts lists - C20 and C21 are 'Film .22 /tF, 100V, 20%', and the 250425-01 list gives 'Film Rdl .22/iF 100V 20%'. Not established: that the film is polyester (the parts lists say only 'Film'), and the 63 VAC working class.

children.name: Mica capacitor
children.description: A capacitor built from thin sheets of natural muscovite mica with vacuum-deposited aluminium or silver counter-electrodes. Superb temperature stability and high dielectric strength, too expensive and too fragile for general use, so mica was reserved for precision and high-voltage niches in equipment of the era.
children.note: Mica was being displaced by film and ceramic in mass-market consumer boards by the 1980s; the sputtered metal-insulator-metal mica construction is a later, higher-reliability form.

children.name: Trimmer and variable capacitors
children.description: Small adjustable capacitors used to compensate or trim a circuit. On C64-family boards a trimmer capacitor sits in the crystal oscillator's load network, pulling the frequency exactly onto the NTSC or PAL colour subcarrier; later Commodore boards replaced the earlier adjustable resistor with this capacitor trim.

facts.label: Range
facts.value: a few pF to tens of pF

facts.label: Function
facts.value: crystal load-network trim; swapped in for R27 on later boards

children.name: Air-gap / film trimmer capacitor
children.description: Two sets of interdigitated metal plates with an adjustable overlap, separated by air or a thin film. Turning the screw changes the overlap and therefore the capacitance continuously, letting the factory trim the oscillator to the exact subcarrier frequency. The dielectric is air, which is why these parts are stable and non-drifting.
children.note: The exact trim capacitor reference designator on the 250407 is uncertain to me; the service manual confirms R27 is the adjustable resistor and the later boards use a capacitive trim in the same role.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: interdigitated plates, air or film dielectric

children.name: Stator and rotor plates
children.description: The trimmer's rotor is a small disc of alumina ceramic, silver-metallised on one face through a spiral or interdigitated pattern. Turning the screw rotates the disc against a fixed plate, so the overlapping metallised area - and hence the capacitance - changes continuously.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: alumina ceramic with a silver counter-electrode, air gap

children.note: Not established: that this is the rotor and stator geometry, the spiral or interdigitated silver pattern, and the continuous overlap-to-capacitance relationship. The service manual lists CT-1 as 'Trimmer 7.7-40pF' but does not describe its construction, and the manual's PLLC replacement notes point to it as a variable.

Not established: a trimmer capacitor in the crystal load network pulling exactly onto the NTSC or PAL subcarrier on the 250407, the few-pF to tens-of-pF range, and replacement of the earlier adjustable resistor R27 with this capacitor on later boards.

mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.name: Alumina rotor plate material
mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.description: The rotor disc is alumina, polished and metallised with a spiral or interdigitated silver pattern. Alumina is used because it is dimensionally stable, machinable to a fine finish and a good insulator at the trimmer's working voltage.
mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.note: Not established: alumina as the rotor material, its polish and metallisation, and its role as a good insulator at the trimmer's working voltage. No document consulted describes trimmer rotor plates.

mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.name: Muscovite mica, heat-split into sheets
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.description: Natural muscovite is mined in large crystal books from pegmatites and delaminated by heating and cementing against a hot plate, so it splits along its perfect basal cleavage into micrometre-thick, optically flat sheets. The crystal's naturally layered atomic structure gives a very uniform, very thin, very stable dielectric when split this way.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.name: Drawn tantalum wire
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.description: The anode lead is fine drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the sintered pellet, drawn by the same machinery as refractory metals for furnace leads. Whether the anode body is built from reduced metallic powder or from sintered oxide powder, the specification is the same: extremely high purity, sub-micron, high surface area. Impurities here are the defect mechanism that causes tantalum dielectric failures, and every stage from columbite-tantalite concentrate to powder discards most of the feed, which is why a tantalum capacitor carried a high metal cost per cubic centimetre even in 1982.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Working electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: The conducting liquid that soaks the separator and carries current between the oxide and the cathode: boric or phosphoric acid dissolved in ethylene glycol, dimethylformamide or dimethyl sulfoxide. The solvent must wet the porous separator without dissolving or attacking the oxide, and the acid concentration sets the oxide's equilibrium thickness.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.note: Not established: dimethyl sulphoxide as a working electrolyte solvent. The documented non-solid systems are borax (ethylene glycol with boric acid) and the organic solvents DMF, DMA and gamma-butyrolactone. The conductivity figure of tens to hundreds of mS/cm is likewise unsourced.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.name: Separator (paper or polyolefin)
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.description: A porous, electrolyte-wicking separator keeping the foils apart while letting current through. Bleached kraft paper was still the standard for most 1980s aluminium electrolytics; low-porosity oriented polypropylene or polyethylene sleeves were the premium, longer-life alternative.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.note: Paper was still the volume material in 1982; polypropylene separators had been commercial for years but were not yet dominant.

facts.label: 1982 default
facts.value: bleached kraft paper; PE/PP sleeves for higher-reliability parts

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: the separator is the main leakage path and electrolyte reservoir

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Silicone rubber bung
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: Heat-cured silicone rubber, chosen because it stays soft and chemically inert in contact with the acid electrolyte for decades. Silicone is a siloxane polymer built on a quartz-derived silicon-oxygen backbone.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.note: Not established: heat-cured grade, and staying soft and chemically inert against the acid electrolyte for decades in these bungs.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.name: Barium titanate dielectric powder
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.description: The heart of the MLCC: sub-micron BaTiO3 crystallites, the only powder that has a very high dielectric constant AND survives the high-temperature processing. Chemistry is shifted from pure BaTiO3 by dopants to move the Curie point below room temperature, giving a Class II (X7R/Z5U) part with high capacitance that still decays with temperature.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.note: Not established: the 0.2-1 um particle size attributed to early-1980s X7R powder. What is documented is the class 2 material set and its codes - barium titanate with aluminium silicate, magnesium silicate and aluminium oxide additives, permittivity 200 to 14000, X7R -55 to +125 C at plus or minus 15 %, Z5U +10 to +85 C at +22/-56 % - and a barium titanate Curie temperature of 120-130 C with dielectric constants to 7000, or 15000 over a narrow range. Those are material-class figures; they are not a figure for any particular commercial grade.

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ~0.2-1 um; coarse-grain BaTiO3 was typical of early-1980s X7R

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.name: Tape-casting slurry (powder + frit + binder)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.description: The BaTiO3 powder is blended with a glass frit - an aid to sintering and to dielectric strength at the electrode interface - and an organic binder into a homogeneous, flowable slip. In 1982 this was an acrylic or PVA binder in water, or a cellulose ester in an organic solvent; fully water-based PVA systems became dominant later.

facts.label: Glass frit
facts.value: ~5 % by weight of the ceramic body

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.note: Not established: the glass frit fraction of about 5 % by weight of the ceramic body, and the specific 1982 binder systems. What is documented is that the casting suspension is the powder with a suitable binder.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.green-sheet.name: Unfired MLCC green sheet (cast dielectric tape)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.green-sheet.description: The tape-casting slurry doctor-bladed onto a moving polyester carrier and dried to a flexible unfired tape: BaTiO3 powder with glass frit in an organic binder. This sheet, printed with electrode paste and stacked, becomes the dielectric layers of the fired capacitor.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: cast slurry dried to a flexible unfired tape (green layer)

facts.label: Slurry system
facts.value: ceramic powder + solvent + dispersant + binder + plasticizer

facts.label: Capability
facts.value: films as thin as 5 um producible by tape casting

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.green-sheet.note: Established: the slurry composition, the cast slurry being called a green layer or green sheet (not a colour), drying to a strippable green tape, and the 1947 capacitor origin with 5 um capability. Not established: the 1982 sheet thickness for these parts (see the tape-cast note). Distinct from the slurry (flowable slip carrying solvent) and from the fired ceramic (dense dielectric): the solvent leaves on drying and the binder on firing, so merging would lose that sequence. REFILE exception (a): this sheet BECOMES the part's dielectric layers; the binder burnout and sintering that convert the unfired tape into dense BaTiO3 are modelled only at stack level (stack-laminate, belt-kiln), so the sheet-to-dielectric finishing step is unmodelled.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.name: Wiper alloy
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.description: A nickel-alloy or precious-metal spring contact rubbing on the RuO2 film. Because the cermet element is hard, the wiper is deliberately the sacrificial element and is made of a soft, wear-resistant alloy.
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.note: A springy phosphor bronze wiper moving over the resistive element is documented for potentiometers. Not established: nickel-alloy or precious-metal wipers on a cermet trimmer, and the sacrificial-wear design argument.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: RuO2 cermet resistive paste
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: The resistive phase is sub-micron ruthenium dioxide powder blended with a lead-borosilicate glass frit and an organic vehicle (butyl acetate / terpineol) into a thixotropic paste. Its sheet resistance is a known function of powder loading, so a given RuO2 fraction sets a given ohms-per-square.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: The paste construction is documented: the resistive ceramic phase is mixed with sintered powdered glass and a carrier liquid so the composite can be screen-printed, and the composite is fused at about 850 C. Ruthenium oxide is listed among the cermet conductors used. Not established: the 0.1-0.5 um RuO2 particle size, the lead-borosilicate glass frit specific to the 1980s, the butyl acetate / terpineol vehicle, and the 10 ohm/sq to 1 Mohm/sq sheet-resistance range.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Resistance alloy wire (NiCr / FeCr / CuNi)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Nichrome has the highest resistivity of the common resistance alloys and so minimises the wire length needed; constantan (CuNi) is used where a lower temperature coefficient matters more.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: Nichrome is documented as the usual winding wire. Not established: that it has the highest resistivity of the common resistance alloys, and that constantan is chosen where a lower temperature coefficient matters more - no constantan figure appears in the source consulted. Note also that the source gives two different Nichrome compositions, 80 Ni / 20 Cr and 60 Ni / 12 Cr / 26 Fe / 2 Mn, melting at 1350-1420 C.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Steatite bobbin material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Steatite, a compacted and fired magnesium silicate, was the classic low-cost bobbin and ceramic insulator material: it machines green, fires to a hard white body and is cheap.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: That the winding core is ceramic - along with plastic or fibreglass - is documented. Not established: steatite specifically, and its green-machinability and firing behaviour. No source consulted names a magnesium-silicate bobbin for a wirewound resistor.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: NiCr resistance alloy
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: 80/20 nickel-chromium, or 75/25 iron-chromium, evaporated or sputtered from a heated wire or boat in a vacuum bell. NiCr is chosen for its bulk resistivity (~1.1 uohm-m) and, critically, for having a near-zero temperature coefficient of resistivity.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Chromite ore and the ferrochrome made from it are metal.chromite and metal.chromium. South Africa supplied the majority of the chrome ore consumed by the Western electronics industry in 1982.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Termination cap material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A nickel-plated steel or aluminium cap, crimped onto the lead and forming the low-resistance joint to the film. Metal film parts are always nickel-plated leads: the plating has to be uniform for the part to be consistent.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Not established: the cap alloy, the crimping, and the requirement that the plating be uniform for consistency. Nothing consulted describes axial metal film end caps.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Metal-film substrate material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Metal film resistors need a very flat and very uniform substrate because the film resistance is set by the length of the deposited track, not by the substrate geometry. Alumina ceramic bar or a flat ceramic tube is used for that flatness.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Not established: alumina ceramic bar or flat ceramic tube as the substrate, and the flatness argument. The general need for a smooth uniform substrate follows from the film resistance depending on track length, but no source consulted names the material.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Composition mix (graphite + clay + binder)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A stiffer, higher-carbon paste than the film slurry. Because it is bulk rather than surface-conductive, the resistance is set by the geometry of the moulded rod itself, not by a pattern on its skin.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The mix itself is documented: the resistive element is a mixture of finely powdered carbon and an insulating material, usually ceramic, held together by a resin, with resistance set by the fill-to-carbon ratio and higher carbon giving lower resistance. Not established: that this particular mix used clay rather than another ceramic, or phenolic rather than another resin.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Resistor slurry (carbon + clay + binder)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Carbon black mixed with china clay as a diluent and a phenolic binder in alcohol to a printable paste. Clay fraction is the coarse knob on resistance; binder keeps the film from flaking off the tube.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: That a carbon film gives lower noise than a carbon composition resistor because of the precise distribution of the pure graphite without binding is documented, and that a carbon film is deposited on an insulating substrate with a helix cut in it. Not established: china clay as the diluent, phenolic binder in alcohol, and the claim that clay fraction is the coarse knob on resistance - the composition-resistor text makes that point for the bulk mix, not for a printed film.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Petroleum residuum (heavy oil feed)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The heaviest fraction of an atmospheric or vacuum refinery distillation: a viscous, bituminous, aromatic-rich residue. It was the classical feedstock for furnace black, but from the 1950s onwards natural gas was the cheaper and cleaner alternative, and a carbon-black plant of 1982 could run on either.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: this feed as the heaviest viscous bituminous aromatic-rich refinery fraction, the 1950s displacement by cheaper cleaner natural gas, and either-feed operation of a 1982 carbon-black plant.

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pi.name: Ink pigment
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pi.description: The value marking pigment is carbon black for dark parts and azo or phthalocyanine colour for bright ones, in a resin vehicle that will not be attacked by the board cleaning solvents.
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pi.note: The carbon-black furnace that makes this pigment is mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-film.powder.carbon-black, linked here by id.

mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.pegmatit.name: Pegmatite host rock
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.pegmatit.description: Mica books grow in the giant granitic pegmatites of the Precambrian shield - Minas Gerais in Brazil, Rajasthan in India, Madagascar, and in the United States the Appalachian and Spruce Pine districts of North Carolina. It is mined in situ and split, not manufactured. The books are followed underground and extracted by hand, selectively enough that the surrounding pegmatite stays intact; Brazilian, Indian and US districts all supply capacitor-grade mica. Mica is traded in sizes - block for the thickest uses, thins for splitting - and grading and splitting, not mining, account for most of the value in the material.

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.name: Steatite or alumina base
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.description: Low-firing ceramic substrates, steatite (magnesium silicate) or alumina, onto which the high-K layer is applied. Steatite is cheap and fires low; alumina is tougher and better at heat.
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.note: Not established: steatite versus alumina as the base under the high-K layer on these discs, and the cheap-and-low-firing versus tougher-and-better-at-heat tradeoff.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Boric acid in the electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Boric acid sets the oxide chemistry of the anode and, with phosphoric acid, is the reason an aluminium electrolytic has a usable voltage range at all. Commercially it was made from borax, which is mined from evaporite deposits.

facts.label: Key deposits
facts.value: California (US), Turkey, Chile - the US borates led world supply in 1982

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Borax (tincalconite) evaporite
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Sodium tetraborate decahydrate occurs in the playas and evaporite deposits of closed desert basins, where boron-bearing volcanic hot springs have fed an evaporating lake for millions of years. It is mined, not synthesised, in the borate districts.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.name: Bleached kraft paper separator
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.description: A very thin, very porous cellulose tissue wound between the foils. It must be wetted completely by the electrolyte but must not contain ions that would raise the leakage current, so it is washed and bleached before use. Kraft paper separators are why the electrolyte is held in place at all.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.note: Not established: the 20-60 um separator thickness quoted here. The standard construction figure for a capacitor rated up to 100 V is 30-75 um, with duplex paper used at higher ratings.

facts.label: Why paper
facts.value: absorbent, cheap, dimensionally stable when wetted

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Ruthenium dioxide powder
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Ruthenium oxide is one of the conductive ceramic phases mixed into a cermet resistor paste, alongside tantalum nitride, lead oxide and others; it is the conductive phase that carries the current, and the glass phase mixed in with it is the insulator that binds the film and gives it its stability. The paste is screen-printed onto a substrate and fused at about 850 C. Ruthenium's scarcity has been a persistent cost driver for cermet resistors.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: Ruthenium oxide is documented as one of the ceramic cermet conductors used in thick film resistors. Not established, and doubtful as stated: that RuO2 is the only phase that survives to 900 C without oxidising away (tantalum nitride and nickel chromium are in the same list), and that 'the surrounding glass is what actually carries the current' - glass is the insulator in a cermet, the conductive phase carries the current.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Platinum-group ore bearing ruthenium
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Ruthenium occurs almost only as a minor by-product in platinum and nickel ores (Merensky Reef, Sudbury, Norilsk) rather than in a ruthenium ore of its own. It reaches the resistor paste as ammonium ruthenium chloride after a complex refining sequence.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: Coarse chain only; the ammonium ruthenium chloride route is my summary of standard refining practice, not a C64-specific fact.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Merensky Reef and nickel-copper sulphide ores
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Ruthenium and the other platinum-group metals have no ore of their own. They occur at a few parts per million in the Merensky Reef of the Bushveld Complex and in the Sudbury and Norilsk nickel-copper sulphide ores, so the resistor industry bought ruthenium as a refinery by-product at platinum-group prices.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: Not established: a few parts per million occurrence, Bushveld Merensky Reef with Sudbury and Norilsk nickel-copper sulphide ores as the provenance of this paste's ruthenium, and refinery by-product purchase at platinum-group prices.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Talc and soapstone
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Steatite is a mixture of talc with clay. Talc is mined from metamorphosed dolomitic rock and is one of the few minerals still worked in a form close to its natural state.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: Not established: talc with clay as the composition of this steatite, and mining from metamorphosed dolomitic rock in a near-natural state for this feed.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Diluent clay in the composition mix
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A much higher clay fraction than in the film slurry, because a composition resistor has to be a weak conductor in bulk. Kaolin was the traditional diluent, the same mineral as in the film mix.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The substance of the claim is documented: the resistive element is a mixture of finely powdered carbon and an insulating material, usually ceramic, held together by a resin, and the resistance is set by the ratio of the fill material to the carbon. Not established: that the diluent was specifically kaolin.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon black (channel/process black)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Furnace black made by feeding heavy residual oil (or natural gas) into a hot air-cooled furnace so that it impinges and soots on water-cooled steel. Furnace black from petroleum feedstock was the standard conductive phase in resistors by the 1980s.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: furnace black from heavy residual oil versus natural gas impinged as soot on water-cooled steel in a hot air-cooled furnace, and petroleum furnace black as the standard resistor conductive phase by the 1980s.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Kaolin (china clay) diluent
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Hydrated aluminium silicate, crushed and classified to a fine particle size. It is inert and non-conducting, so raising its share raises the sheet resistance of the dried film.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The kaolinite mineral is metal.bauxite.kaolinite and its feldspar parent is facility.electricity.feldspar; both are linked here by id.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Phenolic binder resin in the slurry
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Phenol-formaldehyde, dissolved in alcohol, holds carbon and clay to the tube and survives the 260 C cure. Cured phenolic also serves as the resistor's opaque body coating, which protects the film from humidity.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Some 1980s resistor makers switched the body coating to epoxy; the C64's were visually indistinguishable without a microscope.

mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.name: Para-xylene
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.description: Paraxylene sits in the aromatics complex of a large refinery, separated from a mixed xylene fraction by fractional distillation and adsorption. It is the pivot molecule of the entire polyester industry: 1982 saw PET moving from bottle-grade into film, fibre and capacitor dielectric at once.
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.note: Not established: the Urex and Parex adsorption processes, the aromatics-complex location, and the 1982 shift of PET from bottle grade into film and capacitor dielectric. No document consulted covers paraxylene production.

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.name: Disc body material
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.description: The ceramic body of a high-K disc is a modified barium titanate with a glass phase, on an alumina or steatite base. The dielectric-strength figure of about 2.5 kV per micron of effective thickness is a design guideline for the ceramic, not for the finished part.
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.note: Not established: modified barium titanate with a glass phase as the body composition, and an alumina versus steatite base for these discs. The 2.5 kV per micron figure is a design guideline for the ceramic, not a measured value on the finished part.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.name: Epoxy resin and bisphenol A
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.description: The standard epoxy of the period: bisphenol A condensed with epichlorohydrin, cured with an amine. Both halves are petrochemical, and bisphenol A was the dominant resin for adhesive, coating, printed-board and capacitor sealants alike.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.note: Resin-dipped solid tantalum parts are documented. Not established: that the dip sealant was a bisphenol A epoxy cured with an amine, or that bisphenol A dominated capacitor sealants. No source consulted establishes epoxy or bisphenol A.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.name: Manganese chloride for pyrolysis
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.description: MnCl2 is vapour-decomposed on the hot tantalum surface in a furnace at several hundred degrees, leaving a conformal MnO2 layer that acts as the solid counter-electrode. The chloride is shipped as a hydrate and is hygroscopic, so it had to be kept dry.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.note: Not established: vapour decomposition of MnCl2 on the hot tantalum surface at several hundred degrees giving a conformal MnO2 counter-electrode, and hydrate shipment with hygroscopic handling for this supply.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.name: Base-metal nickel paste
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.description: The internal electrode paste: finely divided nickel in a glass frit and an organic vehicle, screen-printed onto the green sheet and co-fired with the ceramic. Nickel was chosen over silver for cost and over palladium for cost, and it is what let a 0.1 uF 50 V bypass capacitor be sold for a fraction of a cent.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.note: Screen-printing a metal paste that co-fires with the ceramic is documented, and nickel is documented as one of the cheaper base metals later used for internal electrodes. Not established: the sub-micron to 1 um particle size, the low-pO2 co-fire specifically for a nickel electrode, and that nickel was already the dominant 1982 internal electrode - the source dates that change to 1993.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.name: Rare-earth dopant oxides
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.description: Lanthanum, dysprosium and yttrium oxides, ground and sieved to sub-micron, are the donor dopants that set the temperature coefficient of an X7R dielectric. The sub-micron sieve is the whole difficulty: a barium titanate powder wants its additives soluble or finely dispersed so that no second phase forms, and an oxide bought at the separation plant's standard grade arrives as lumps. These are the most expensive few grams on the bill of materials and they were bought by the kilogram, not the tonne, so the MLCC maker was dependent on the same two plants as the television maker for the same handful of elements.

facts.label: Which oxides
facts.value: lanthanum, dysprosium and yttrium, as donor dopants

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ground and sieved to sub-micron, or they will not disperse in the barium titanate

facts.label: Cost position
facts.value: among the most expensive grams in the component, and bought in kilogram quantities

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.note: Not established: lanthanum, dysprosium and yttrium as the donor dopants in the board's MLCC dielectrics, the sub-micron grinding and sieving difficulty, and kilogram-not-tonne purchasing dependent on the same two plants as the television maker.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.name: Titanium dioxide (TiO2) feed
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.description: Ceramic-grade TiO2, made by chlorinating ilmenite or rutile to TiCl4 and re-oxidising, or by sulphuric acid digestion. Low-iron pigment-grade material is used so the fired ceramic has good insulation resistance.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.note: Barium titanate is documented as made by heating barium carbonate and titanium dioxide, so TiO2 is confirmed as a feed. Not established: the chlorination of ilmenite or rutile to TiCl4 and re-oxidation, the sulphuric acid route, low-iron pigment grade for insulation resistance, and the 1982 ilmenite supply geography.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Glass-filled epoxy coat
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The whole array is coated in an epoxy loaded with fine glass or silica, which both seals the tracks and gives the package its mechanical rigidity. The colour body is the colourant in that coat.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.note: Not established: an epoxy loaded with fine glass or silica as the encapsulant, and that the body colour is the colourant in that coat. The small white dot denoting resistance on these packages is not explained by any source consulted.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Nd:YAG laser crystal
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: Neodymium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet was the standard solid-state laser for resistor trimming: a garnet crystal doped with neodymium, pumped optically and emitting at 1.06 microns. The yttrium-aluminium-garnet host is grown from alumina and yttrium oxide.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.note: Not established: neodymium-doped yttrium-aluminium-garnet emitting at 1.06 microns as the trim laser for these networks, and an alumina plus yttrium oxide grown garnet host for this tool.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Atomised silver powder
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: The conductor paste is fine silver flake or powder, not a bulk metal: it has to print as a paste and then fuse into a continuous conductor at 850 C without melting. Domestically mined silver was almost entirely gone by 1982; the metal was bought on the London spot market.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: Mined silver was economically a by-product metal by the 1980s, with Mexico, Peru, the US and Canada still significant districts; metal.silver.ingot carries the refining side.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: atomised or electrolytic silver powder / flake, typically 99.9 %

facts.label: Silver ore
facts.value: argentite Ag2S; by 1982 most world silver was a by-product of Pb-Zn and Cu refining

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Foil metal
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Pure nickel or a nickel-iron-chromium alloy, chosen for a low temperature coefficient of resistivity and for its mechanical stability under tension.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Not established: pure nickel versus nickel-iron-chromium alloy as the foil metal, chosen for low temperature coefficient of resistivity and mechanical stability under tension.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: NiCr foil resistance alloy (wrought strip stock)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Wrought nickel-chromium resistance alloy, melt-cast and rolled to strip for etching into precision foil resistors: typically 80 Ni / 20 Cr, resistivity around 1.1 uohm-m, with a protective chromium-oxide skin. It is bulk strip stock, not evaporated film: its low temperature coefficient and creep strength survive rolling and etching into the resistive element.

facts.label: Protection
facts.value: thermodynamically stable chromium-oxide skin in air

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Established: the NiCr family, the standard compositions, resistivity, melting point and oxide skin. Not established: the exact 1982 precision-foil grade (trade-name Evanohm-type compositions have no verifiable source here) and foil-specific TCR figures. NiCr check: the existing metal-film.nichrome is an evaporated/sputtered thin-film feedstock and wirewound.alloy is drawn wire; both are different manufacturing forms from wrought foil strip, so merging would lose the form and route facts and no merge is proposed. REFILE exception (a): the etched foil becomes the part's resistive element; transfer-and-bond of the etched foil onto its substrate is unmodelled.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Band ink
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Offset printing inks cured onto the epoxy body. The ink is a pigment in an oil and resin vehicle fired at a few hundred degrees so it will not rub off or solvent-attack during board cleaning.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: That the bands were cheaply printed onto tiny components, and that printing technology later made printed numbers more practical, are both documented. Not established: the offset or rotogravure coater, the pigment-in-oil vehicle, and the cure at a few hundred degrees that keeps the bands from rubbing off or solvent attack.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Tinned copper lead wire
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The axial lead is drawn copper wire, cut to length, tinned in a molten tin or tin-lead pot so the resistor dips cleanly in the wave-solder bath. Tinning is what stops the bare copper wire from oxidising between the barrel plating step and the board.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: ~0.6 mm diameter, tinned in a 230-250 C pot

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The 0.6 mm tinned lead is documented, though the source states it for low-power wirewound resistors rather than carbon film: wire leads in low power wirewound resistors are usually between 0.6 and 0.8 mm in diameter and tinned for ease of soldering. Not established: the 230-250 C tin pot temperature, and the specific claim about oxidation between barrel plating and the board.

mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.name: Vacuum-metallised polyester film
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.description: PET pellets are extruded into a cast film, then stretched fast in two perpendicular directions to several times their original length, orienting the polymer chains. That gives a very thin, very uniform, high-tensile dielectric; then a sub-micron metal layer is vacuum-deposited on one or both faces and the metallised film is wound on a core. No separate foil is used - the electrode IS the deposited layer.
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.note: Not established: the 1-6 um film thickness quoted for 1982. The process is documented - biaxial stretching in longitudinal and transverse directions, a vacuum-deposited aluminium metallisation of about 0.03 um on one or both sides, wound onto a mother roll about 1 m wide - and the modern minimum film thickness is quoted as 0.6 um, so a 1982 figure would be thicker, not thinner.

children.name: PET polymerisation
children.description: The film base is polyethylene terephthalate, made by condensing bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate - itself from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid - in a melt polymeriser at ~250-290 C under vacuum. The terephthalic acid came from paraxylene, which came from the aromatics fraction of a steam cracker or a catalytic reformer.

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: melt condensation at ~270 C under vacuum

children.note: Not established: the melt condensation route, the 250-290 C under vacuum, and the bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate intermediate. The one sourced PET fact in hand is the trade names Hostaphan and Mylar and the polyester family classification, which is not a synthesis route.

mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.styren.name: Styrene polymerisation to polystyrene
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.styren.description: Free-radical or ionic polymerisation of styrene, in bulk suspension or emulsion, gives the amorphous thermoplastic. Unmodified polystyrene is brittle and has poor moisture resistance, which is precisely why metalised polystyrene was restricted to sealed precision parts and lost out to polypropylene.
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.styren.note: Not established: brittleness and poor moisture resistance as the reason metallised polystyrene was restricted, and the free-radical or ionic polymerisation route. What is documented is the commercial outcome - polystyrene film could not be made thinner than 10 um and its maximum temperature rating reached only 85 C, so it was largely replaced by polyester; it was valued for high capacitance stability, low dissipation factor, low leakage and a near-zero temperature coefficient.

mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.metall.name: Vacuum metallisation of PS film
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.metall.description: The same vacuum-deposited aluminium electrode as on the polyester film, but on a more delicate substrate: polystyrene outgasses and embrittles under vacuum heat, so the film has to be baked and the deposition kept cool.
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.metall.note: Not established: vacuum-deposited aluminium electrodes on polystyrene film for these parts, polystyrene outgassing and embrittlement under vacuum heat, and the bake plus cool-deposition remedy.

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.name: Pressing, sintering and silver-firing
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.description: BaTiO3 powder is pressed into a disc, sintered at 1200-1300 C, then silver electrode paste is screen-printed onto each face and fired at 700-850 C so the silver is glass-bonded to the ceramic. Only two electrodes exist, so the part cannot cancel its own inductance - the structural reason a disc is useless at radio frequencies and a multilayer is not.

children.name: Disc press and sinter
children.description: A mechanical or hydraulic press blanks the disc to a controlled thickness; the sinter then densifies it and fires on the silver electrodes.
children.note: Not established: mechanical versus hydraulic press blanking to a controlled thickness, and the densify plus fire-on-silver-electrodes sinter sequence for these discs.

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.note: Not established: the 1200-1300 C sinter and the 700-850 C silver electrode fire through the glass frit. What is documented is the construction - the early ceramic disc style was a disc with metallisation on both sides contacted with tinned wires, and the modern disc style is a single-layer disc with a resin coating and through-hole leads. The single-electrode-pair structure is the documented reason a disc has no internal inductance cancellation.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.name: Anodic Ta2O5 formation and MnO2 solid electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.description: The sintered anode is anodised to grow the Ta2O5 dielectric, then coated with manganese dioxide by pyrolysing manganese nitrate: the pellet is dipped into an aqueous nitrate solution and baked at about 250 C to leave the dioxide coat - the classic 1980s solid tantalum part. A sintered silver-paste counter-electrode existed as an alternative construction. Today's conductive-polymer tantalum is a late-1990s development. The anode is anodised at a voltage above its rated working voltage, usually by a factor of 1.5-2, to build a defect-free oxide; the rated voltage of the part is set by that formation step and cannot be adjusted afterwards.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.note: Two divergences from the documented process. The counter-electrode is described as made by pyrolysis of manganese NITRATE, not manganese chloride. And the safety margin between forming voltage and rated voltage for solid MnO2 tantalum is given as typically 2 to 4, not the 1.5-2 quoted here. The anodising step itself is documented: the pellet is submerged in a weak acid, DC is applied, and the total dielectric thickness is set by the final voltage held.

facts.label: Counter-electrode
facts.value: MnO2 from manganese nitrate pyrolysis (standard); sintered Ag paste (alternative)

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: forming voltage sets the working voltage, with a safety margin in oxide thickness of typically 2 to 4 times the rated voltage

children.name: Counter-electrode body
children.description: Below the manganese dioxide sits the original tantalum anode body and its second termination. The layer stack is metal, dielectric, counter-electrode, then a conductive path to the case - all inside an epoxy dip.
children.note: Not established: the metal, dielectric, counter-electrode and conductive-path-to-case layer order for these parts, and enclosure in an epoxy dip.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.name: Tantalum lead, braze and epoxy seal
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.description: The anode lead is drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the sintered pellet, then the assembly is sealed by an epoxy dip. On wet-slug types the hermetic case is glass or a welded metal can with a Teflon ring seal. The part is then marked with its value, rating and the manufacturer.

facts.label: Anode lead
facts.value: drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the pellet

facts.label: Braze
facts.value: silver or silver-graphite drop for the lead joint; Ta-Au braze on some types

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: epoxy dip for solid types; welded metal can for wet-slug types

children.name: Epoxy dip seal
children.description: Solid tantalum parts were sealed by dipping in epoxy and curing, which protects the brittle MnO2/dielectric stack against handling and moisture. Wet-slug parts instead used a welded metal can with a glass or Teflon seal.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.note: Not established: drawn tantalum wire spot-welded to the pellet as the anode lead, silver versus silver-graphite versus Ta-Au braze alternatives, and epoxy dip versus welded metal can with Teflon ring as the seal on the board's tantalum parts.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..name: Capacitor-grade recycling loop
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..description: Because tantalum metal is expensive, tantalum-bearing scrap - rejected capacitors, anode dust, trimmed pellet scrap - was recovered and returned to the powder supply. This is why a 1983-84 shortage hit prices so hard: recycled powder could not be substituted for virgin powder in a dielectric that had to be defect-free.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..note: Not established: recovery of rejected capacitors, anode dust and trimmed pellet scrap into the powder supply, and the 1983-84 shortage mechanism in which recycled powder could not substitute for virgin powder in a defect-free dielectric.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.press.name: Anode pressing and sintering
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.press.description: Powder is blended with a binder and pressed around the wire, then debound and sintered in vacuum or flowing hydrogen at 1200-1400 C. The pressed pellet is deliberately porous - roughly half its volume is void - because that void is where the dielectric forms.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.press.note: Not established: that roughly half the pressed pellet's volume is void. What is documented is that sintering turns the powder into a sponge-like monolithic lattice that is highly porous with a large internal surface area, at 1200-1800 C under vacuum.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.name: Winding on a mandrel and impregnation
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.description: Anode foil, separator and cathode foil are wound together on a rotating mandrel into a compact roll. Electrolyte is then vacuum- or pressure-impregnated into the wound roll, filling every pore and pushing out air, which is what finally gives the part its capacitance.

facts.label: Impregnation
facts.value: vacuum impregnation, repeated 2-4 times to drive out trapped air

facts.label: Slitting
facts.value: cathode foil is slit into two or three ribbons for a multi-section winding

children.name: Winding mandrel
children.description: A polished steel mandrel, often Teflon-coated, on which the foil sandwich is wound. Mandrel diameter and surface finish are set by the smallest foil thickness so the finished pack can be released without creasing.
children.note: Automatic winding is documented. Not established: the mandrel material or its Teflon coating, or that mandrel diameter is set by the smallest foil thickness.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Crimping, sleeving and end-fill bung
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: Aluminium or tinned-copper alloy terminal tabs are crimped onto the anode and cathode edges of the wound pack. The pack is then sleeved - PVC heat-shrink or a printed cardboard outer - and sealed at the end with a rubber or PVC bung that retains the electrolyte against its expansion over temperature. The paper and foil layers you see when you cut one open are the winding itself.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: crimped Al or Cu alloy tab; anode polarity marked on the sleeve

facts.label: Sleeve
facts.value: PVC heat-shrink or printed cardboard outer

children.name: End-fill bung
children.description: A rubber or PVC disc that fills the end of the sleeve and retains the electrolyte against thermal expansion and the internal pressure generated during burn-in. It is the visible rubber disc at the base of a radial electrolytic.

children.name: Aluminium terminal tab
children.description: A soft aluminium or aluminium-alloy tab, crimped onto the foil edge. Pure aluminium is used because it is the only metal that will not form a galvanic or resistive joint with the foil it must touch.

facts.label: Alloy limit
facts.value: Fe and Si above a few tenths of a per cent make the tab hard and prone to sludge in the electrolyte

facts.label: Tab metal
facts.value: capacitor-grade aluminium, purer than structural grade

children.note: Terminal welding to lead-out terminals during winding is documented. Not established: crimping, and the claim that pure aluminium is used because it will not form a galvanic or resistive joint with the foil, or the iron and silicon limits of a few tenths of a per cent.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging.name: Ageing and burn-in
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging.description: Finished parts are held at an elevated temperature under DC bias so the oxide re-thickens and the leakage current settles: typically 1-2x the rated voltage at 85-125 C for hours to days. A 1980s capacitor therefore arrives already partly formed, which is why an electrolytic recovered from a two-year-old Commodore machine often measures better than a brand-new one.

facts.label: Burn-in
facts.value: ~1-2x rated voltage at 85-125 C, hours to days

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: reduces initial leakage and stabilises capacitance

children.name: Burn-in chamber
children.description: A temperature-controlled rack of trays in which finished parts are held at temperature and bias. A good capacitor plant in 1982 might burn in for hours or days, which is why vintage electrolytics so often arrive already formed.
children.note: Not established: a temperature-controlled rack of trays holding finished parts at temperature and bias, and hours-or-days burn-in at a 1982 capacitor plant for this supply.

children.name: Capacitance and leakage test
children.description: Parts are tested for capacitance, dissipation factor and leakage at rated temperature. Rejection rates in a commodity 10 uF 25 V part were small but non-zero, and every rejected part was a loss of scrap aluminium. A bridge or LCR meter at rated frequency and temperature gives capacitance and dissipation factor, and a DC bias step gives leakage; rejection on leakage is what catches a pinhole in the oxide, the classic failure mode of a fresh electrolytic.
children.note: 100 % final measurement of capacitance, leakage current and impedance after post-forming is documented, and the dissipation factor is documented as the datasheet alternative to ESR. Not established: testing at rated temperature specifically, the commodity rejection rate, and that leakage rejection catches a pinhole in the oxide.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging.note: Not established: the 1-2x rated voltage at 85-125 C for hours to days regime for the board's electrolytics, and the claims that a 1980s part arrives already partly formed and that a two-year-old recovered part often measures better than new.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.name: Cathode foil rolling
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.description: High-purity aluminium rolled to a few tens of microns, often lightly etched, slit into ribbons for the winding. It uses the same aluminium as the anode but a looser specification, because no dielectric quality depends on it.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Anodic formation (the real dielectric)
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: The etched foil is made the anode in a phosphoric or boric acid bath at 90-200 V DC, growing a barrier-type aluminium oxide layer tens of nanometres thick. The rated working voltage of the finished capacitor is just the voltage the oxide can hold, so higher ratings need a thicker oxide and hence less capacitance for the same area.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.note: Not established: the 90-200 V DC forming voltage quoted for parts rated 6-50 V. What is documented is the relationship - oxide thickness proportional to forming voltage, 14 nm at 10 V and 140 nm at 100 V, amorphous oxide 1.4 nm/V against 1.0 nm/V crystalline - together with the standardised safety margin that puts the forming voltage above the rated voltage.

facts.label: Forming voltage
facts.value: ~90-200 V DC for parts rated 6-50 V

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Anode foil from re-melted foil-mill scrap
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: Rolled foil offcuts, edge trim and rejected capacitor-grade foil were re-smelted in a holding furnace and re-rolled into fresh anode foil rather than going back to the general scrap stream. The other half of the loop is primary metal: alumina from bauxite, smelted in a Hall-Heroult cell by dissolving it in molten cryolite and electrolytising at 950-970 C to 99.7 % pure cathodes. That closed loop is why capacitor makers were in effect recycling their own aluminium, and why an aluminium price move showed up in 1982 capacitor prices with a lag.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.note: Cryolite is synthesised from hydrofluoric acid and alumina, and the hydrofluoric acid historically came from fluorspar mined in Mexico, South Africa and China. Prime foil from the primary smelter was still used for the tightest-tolerance parts and I cannot say which proportion applied to Commodore's 1982 supply.

facts.label: Hall-Heroult cell
facts.value: alumina in molten cryolite at ~950-970 C

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.name: Tape casting to green sheets
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.description: The slip is doctor-bladed onto a moving polyester carrier film to a controlled dry thickness. This single step sets the eventual capacitance density, because capacitance is dielectric thickness divided by the number of electrode layers stacked.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.note: Not established: the 5-20 um green-sheet thickness attributed to early-1980s parts. What is documented is that a thin ceramic foil is cast from a suspension of the powder with a suitable binder, and that dielectric layer thickness fell from 4 um in 1995 to 1 um in 2005 and about 0.5 um by 2010, with the layer thickness limited by the powder grain size.

facts.label: Green sheet thickness
facts.value: ~1-10 um; early-1980s parts often cast 5-20 um

children.name: Moving carrier belt
children.description: The green sheet is carried on a continuous polyester belt and dried in a short oven as the doctor blade lays it down, so the green thickness is set by blade clearance against a moving web rather than by a single-shot cast.
children.note: Not established: the continuous polyester carrier belt and the short in-line drying oven. No document consulted describes the tape-casting line layout.

children.name: Doctor blade
children.description: A precisely-ground steel or ceramic blade with a controlled edge angle, set to micrometres over the belt. The single most important tool in MLCC making: it sets layer thickness and therefore capacitance density.
children.note: Casting a thin ceramic foil from a powder-and-binder suspension to a controlled thickness is documented. Not established: the doctor blade itself - a ground steel or ceramic blade set to micrometres over a moving belt - and its description as the single most important tool in the manufacture.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.name: Stacking, lamination and debinding
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.description: The printed green sheets are stacked offset so every sheet's electrode lands alternately on the two opposed faces, then compressed in a hydraulic laminator and the organic binder burned out slowly. The result is a monolithic bar of hundreds of ceramic layers with the electrodes sealed inside.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: ~10-60 active layers for a 1982 0.1 uF 50 V part

facts.label: Debinding
facts.value: slow ramp 200-400 C to avoid cracking the stack

children.name: Hydraulic laminator
children.description: A heated hydraulic press that stacks and consolidates hundreds of sheets at once, aligned by registration pins. This is the step that turns a pile of loose printed film into one solid bar.
children.note: Stacking and solidifying by pressure is documented. Not established: a heated hydraulic press, registration pins, or that this is the step that turns loose printed film into a solid bar.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.note: Not established: the 10-60 active layer count for a 1982 0.1 uF 50 V part, the lamination pressure in tens of MPa, and the 200-400 C debind ramp. What is documented is that the printed sheets are stacked in the required number of layers, solidified by pressure, and that the binder is burnt out of the stack after cutting.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.name: End terminations (nickel + solderable outer)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.description: After firing, the two exposed end faces are terminated with a conducting band that collects current from the hundreds of buried electrodes. In 1982 this was a fired-on or sputtered nickel layer with a solderable silver or tin outer layer, or a simple dipped solder band. The C64 boards were wave-soldered in tin-lead, so the termination had to wet 63/37 solder.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.note: The nickel barrier plus a solderable outer layer is well established; which outer-layer option Commodore's capacitor supplier used in 1982 is not.

facts.label: 1982 termination
facts.value: Ni barrier with Ag or Ni-Sn outer layer, or dipped tin-lead solder

facts.label: Modern difference
facts.value: pure sintered Ni-Sn terminations with no precious metal are today's standard

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..name: Epoxy lock
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..description: After alignment a drop of epoxy is flowed over the adjuster so the setting cannot drift in service. On a machine with no calibration facility this trimmer is effectively a one-time factory adjustment for forty years. It is a deliberate, destructive lock: once the trim is set on the factory line that trimmer is not adjustable again.
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..note: Not established: the epoxy lock and the account of the trimmer as a one-time factory adjustment. That trimmers are for infrequent adjustment during manufacture or repair is documented; the destructive epoxy lock is not, in any source consulted.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Laser trimming of the network
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: An excimer or Nd:YAG laser ablates slots in each printed resistor until a closed-loop bridge calls out the right value. Bulk trimming can be 'slug' or 'v-cut' (pushing a wedge of resistive material aside) rather than ablating material away.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.note: Trimming is documented: the resistance of thick film resistors after manufacture is not highly accurate and is trimmed to value by abrasive or laser trimming. Not established: the excimer and Nd:YAG laser choice, the v-cut or slug bulk-trim alternative, a rate of 10,000 networks per hour, and a tolerance of 0.1 %. The documented history goes the other way on tolerance - thick film resistors started at 5 % and improved to 2 % or 1 %.

children.name: Laser trimming system
children.description: A pulsed laser head over a moving substrate with an in-line ohmmeter, cutting and re-measuring thousands of times per second. Excimer lasers were used for fine-resolution cuts on thick films.
children.note: Not established: the pulsed laser head with in-line ohmmeter measuring thousands of times per second, and the excimer laser for fine-resolution cuts. The source establishes only that thick film resistors are trimmed by laser among other methods.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Epoxy potting and marking
