mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The trimmed network is coated in a fire-resistant epoxy or phenolic varnish that also carries the colour code - here a small white dot or body colour denoting the resistance. Glass-filled epoxy was the standard SIP encapsulant.

children.name: Lead frame
children.description: The array's leads are formed from a copper-alloy lead frame, plated in tin or solder, so the package can be inserted on a 2.54 mm pitch and wave-soldered.
children.note: The 8-pin and 10-pin single-in-line form factor on a 2.54 mm pitch is documented by the parts list. Not established: that the leads come from a copper-alloy lead frame plated in tin or solder, and that the package is wave-soldered.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.note: The on-board network is documented in the primary parts list as a Bourns part - RP1,RP2 '330, 8 Pin (Bourns No. 4308R-102-330)', RP3 '3.3KQ, 8 Pin (Bourns No. 4308R-101-332)', RP4 '3.3KQ, 10 Pin' - which settles the single-in-line pin count but not the encapsulant. Not established: a fire-resistant epoxy or phenolic varnish carrying the colour code, and that glass-filled epoxy was the standard SIP encapsulant.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Thick-film conductor metallisation
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A base-metal paste of finely divided silver or copper in a glass frit, screen-printed and fired at ~850 C to form the end lands, jumpers and common bus the resistive tracks connect to. Silver-palladium pastes were common in this era; copper pastes needed a nitrogen atmosphere to avoid oxidising.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: The glass-frit conductor paste fired at about 850 C is documented. Not established: that the base metal was silver or silver-palladium with copper pastes needing a nitrogen atmosphere, and the late-1980s dating of nickel-bearing pastes.

facts.label: Base metal
facts.value: Ag or Ag-Pd (Ni-Pd-Ag common from the late 1980s)

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Etched metal foil roll
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A strip of pure or alloy foil is rolled to a very tight radius on a mandrel and acid-etched to remove most of it, leaving fine islands of metal in series across the roll. The number of islands, not the sheet resistivity, sets the resistance.

children.name: Selective acid etch
children.description: The rolled foil is immersed in a ferric-nitrate or nitric-acid etch that removes most of it, leaving a fine grid of metal islands. Resistance is then set by the number of islands in the path, which is why foil resistors have their characteristic very high, very stable resistance values.
children.note: Not established: ferric-nitrate versus nitric-acid etch removing most of the rolled foil to a grid of islands, with island count setting the resistance and giving very high very stable values.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Not established: mandrel rolling to a tight radius followed by acid etching to fine islands in series, about 1000 islands per inch, and islands-not-sheet-resistivity setting the resistance. Whether foil resistors appear on the 250407 at all is also not established.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Vitreous enamel coating
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: The wound wire is coated in a glassy enamel and baked, which is why wirewounds are glassy-bodied. Continuous operation above about 200 C needs cement or silicone instead.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: Not established: glassy enamel coating and baking as the finish on these wirewounds, and the about-200 C switchover to cement or silicone for continuous operation.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Laser scribing of the spiral
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A pulsed ruby or Nd:YAG laser ablates a thin groove across the film, lengthening the resistive path. A closed-loop measuring bridge runs thousands of cuts per second until the value converges. This - not a mechanical wheel - is what buys the 0.1-1 percent tolerance.

facts.label: Achievable tolerance
facts.value: 0.1-1 %, vs +/-5 % for a cut carbon film

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: The temperature coefficient is documented exactly: a metal film resistor cut by a helix through a NiCr coating gives 0.5 %, 1 % or 2 % tolerance and a temperature coefficient generally between 50 and 100 ppm/K. Not established: the 0.1-1 % tolerance claimed, the 1000-10000 parts per hour trim rate, and the claim that laser scribing rather than a mechanical wheel is what buys the precision - the source describes the helix cut without saying which tool makes it.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Compression moulding
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The mix is pressed in a matched-metal die at tens of tonnes to fill a slug shaped like a small pill, then baked. End caps of tin or brass are pressed on after cure.

children.name: Matched metal die
children.description: A matched-metal compression die with a cavity shaped like the finished slug. The cavity is chrome plated to survive the abrasive mix and the pressure.
children.note: Not established: matched-metal construction with a slug-shaped cavity, and chrome plating to survive the abrasive mix and the pressing pressure.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: pressing at tens of tonnes in a matched-metal die to a small-pill slug, baking at 150-200 C, and tin versus brass end caps pressed on after cure for these parts.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Axial lead termination (electroplate)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A lead is pushed down each end of the tube through the carbon film, and the assembly is barrel-plated in an electroless or electrolytic nickel bath so the film and lead make a low-resistance, solderable joint. In 1982 this was almost always nickel, sometimes with a thin silver flash.

children.name: Electroplating line (sulfamate / alkaline nickel)
children.description: Racks of resistors are plated in a barrel or belt line, then rinsed and dried. Plate thickness is the mechanical anchor that stops the lead being pulled out.
children.note: Not established: barrel or belt plating of racks of resistors, and the 2-5 um nickel plate thickness. No document consulted describes axial resistor plating lines.

children.name: Electrolytic nickel plating bath
children.description: The lead and film are plated in a sulfamate or a Watts-type nickel bath. A sulfonamide-derived depolarising agent suppresses hydrogen evolution, so the deposit is ductile and the lead does not become brittle - which matters because a brittle lead snaps inside the resistor.
children.note: Not established: the sulfamate or pyrophosphate bath, the sulfonamide depolariser, the 30-50 g/L nickel, and the few A/dm2 current density. Plausible plating practice, but no source consulted supports it.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: leads pushed down each tube end through the carbon film, barrel plating in an electroless versus electrolytic nickel bath to a low-resistance solderable joint, and nickel-almost-always with an occasional thin silver flash in 1982.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Value trimming (abrasive wheel)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A diamond wheel cuts a narrow slot through the film from the end of the tube, lengthening the resistive path a few micrometres at a time until the measured resistance hits the middle of the tolerance band. This is why carbon film resistors are called 'film' and why their tolerance is fixed after firing rather than before.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Modern carbon film is still trimmed this way; laser trimming only ever made sense for thin film.

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: abrasive slot, NOT a laser scribing cut

children.name: Abrasive cut-off wheel
children.description: A thin abrasive wheel, run at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute, cuts a slot through the film. Each pass lengthens the resistive path slightly; a few passes reach value.
children.note: Abrasive trimming is documented, as is cutting a helix in the film to create the resistive path. Not established: the thin abrasive wheel running at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute, or that each pass lengthens the path slightly.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Offset-printed colour-code bands
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The value and tolerance rings are printed on the epoxy body by an offset (rotogravure / dry-offset) coater using inks fired onto the surface. Three bands give significant figures, one multiplier, one tolerance. A 5 percent part gets a gold band; 1 percent gets brown.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Bands are printed AFTER the part is trimmed and moulded - the trim determines the value, the print only reports it.

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, grey, white; gold, silver

facts.label: Method
facts.value: offset printing, ink cured onto epoxy

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Epoxy moulding of the resistor body
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The resistor is placed in a transfer tool and encapsulated in epoxy resin cured at ~150-175 C for several minutes. Epoxy is chosen because it shrinks little and does not stress the film on cooling.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: transfer-tool encapsulation in epoxy, the 150-175 C cure for several minutes, and the low-shrinkage argument. No document consulted describes how an axial resistor body is moulded. Note that the service manual's own note - 'ALL RESISTORS ARE 1/4 WATT 5% UNLESS OTHERWISE SPECIFIED' - and its separate line 'RESISTORS - All are carbon 1/4 watt, 5% unless noted' establish only the rating and the carbon technology, not the encapsulant.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Tube extrusion and firing
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Plasticised alumina is extruded through a die to a tube, cut to length on a flying saw, and fired in a tunnel kiln. Density is controlled so the film sees a reproducible surface.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: extrusion of plasticised alumina to a tube, the flying saw, and the 1500-1650 C sintering. A carbon film is documented as deposited on an insulating substrate, but the substrate's manufacture is not described in any source consulted.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Refractory kiln furniture
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: Alumina setters and shelves carrying the fired substrates through the kiln, themselves made from tabular alumina. Furnace furniture consumption is a real cost line in ceramics, and it comes from the same alumina as the substrate.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: Not established: alumina setters and shelves of tabular alumina carrying these substrates through the kiln, and furnace-furniture consumption as a real cost line on this firing.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Aluminium oxide abrasive
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The standard grinding abrasive of the era, made by calcining alumina. Synthetic diamond was used only where the cut had to be finer.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: aluminium oxide as the standard grinding abrasive, or that synthetic diamond was used only where a finer cut was needed. No document consulted describes trim wheel abrasives.

mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-spl.name: Heat-and-cement splitting and ruby splitting
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-spl.description: A mica book is mounted on a hot plate; a hot blade of mica is pressed onto it with a cement stick, which drives a wedge along the perfect basal cleavage and peels off a sheet a few microns thick. Repeated, it yields hundreds of optically flat sheets from one crystal, and it is the labour-intensive step that made mica capacitors expensive.
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-spl.note: Splitting is done by hand against a hot plate; automation did not reach the industry in this period.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: thousands of sheets per cubic foot of rough

children.name: Hot knife and cement stick
children.description: A heated mica blade driven by a cement stick along the cleavage plane. The blade has to be hot enough to part the sheets without charring the cement, and both blade and stick are specialist consumables of the splitting trade.
children.note: Not established: a heated blade driven by a cement stick along the cleavage plane, the hot-enough-without-charring condition, and whether mica capacitors on this board used split muscovite at all.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Glycol-ether solvent from petrochemistry
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Ethylene glycol and the glycol ethers used as high-voltage capacitor solvents were derived from ethylene oxide, itself made by oxidising ethylene from a steam cracker. They replaced the glycol-ester electrolytes of the 1950s because they dissolve the anode oxide without attacking it.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: crude -> steam cracking -> ethylene -> ethylene oxide -> glycol ether

children.name: Ethylene glycol ethers from ethylene oxide
children.description: Ethylene oxide is made by direct oxidation of ethylene over a silver or chromite catalyst, then reacts with an alcohol to give the glycol ether. The solvent chemistry of an aluminium electrolytic is therefore set two or three steps downstream of a steam cracker.
children.note: Not established: direct oxidation of ethylene over a silver or chromite catalyst, and the subsequent alcoholysis to the glycol ether. No source consulted establishes ethylene oxide.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.note: Ethylene glycol with boric acid as the standard borax electrolyte, and DMF, DMA and gamma-butyrolactone as the anhydrous organics, are documented. Not established: the glycol-ether route from a steam cracker, and the claim that these replaced glycol-ester electrolytes of the 1950s.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.name: Solid-state BaTiO3 synthesis
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.description: Barium carbonate and titanium dioxide are ball-milled with the dopants in water to a homogeneous slurry, then calcined in a kiln at about 1050-1200 C. The carbonate decomposes and the perovskite BaTiO3 crystallises. The mass is reground and wet-milled with a dispersant down to the target particle size.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.note: Not established: the 1050-1200 C calcination temperature and the zirconia or nylon wet-milling detail. What is documented is the reaction itself - barium titanate manufactured by heating barium carbonate and titanium dioxide, the reaction proceeding via liquid phase sintering.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.name: Donor / acceptor doping
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.description: Trivalent donor dopants (La2O3, Dy2O3, Y2O3) or pentavalent acceptors (Nb2O5, Ta2O5, Sb2O5) are added during calcination. Donors leave the ceramic 'depleted' so the grains sit uniformly in the paraelectric phase at room temperature, which gives the stable, moderate-loss X7R curve. Acceptor dopants raise the Curie point so the material stays ferroelectric and gives a much higher, more temperature-sensitive Z5U.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.note: The physics is standard ceramics; the specific dopant-to-Class assignments are my summary and are flagged medium.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.name: Firing in a continuous belt kiln
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.description: The blanks go through a continuous belt or pusher kiln under a controlled low oxygen partial pressure, so the ceramic sinters dense and hermetic while the nickel internal electrodes are not oxidised away. Density matters enormously: a porous body lets moisture attack the electrode stack and destroys the insulation resistance. The atmosphere is a forming gas or nitrogen with an oxygen partial pressure held just low enough that nickel does not oxidise and high enough that the organic binder burns off cleanly; getting that window right is the hardest part of base-metal MLCC manufacture.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.note: Not established: the low oxygen partial pressure and forming-gas or nitrogen atmosphere, and the >99.5 % theoretical density figure. What is documented is the order of operations and the temperature - binder burnt out after cutting, then sintering at 1200-1450 C to give the final mainly crystalline structure. The atmosphere requirement is tied to which electrode metal is used and is not stated in the source.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: low pO2 / forming gas or N2

children.name: Kiln heating elements
children.description: Silicon-carbide or nichrome elements in a continuous belt kiln held at ~1300 C for hours. Long soaks at high temperature are what drive the ceramic to theoretical density.
children.note: The 1200-1450 C sinter is documented. Not established: that the kiln is heated by silicon-carbide or nichrome elements, or the hours-long soak. No element type or soak time appears in any source consulted.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.name: Screen printing through a photoemulsion
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.description: A stainless-steel mesh stretched over a frame, coated in photosensitive emulsion, contact-exposed through a film or direct-imaged artwork, developed, and then the paste squeegeed through the open areas onto the substrate. Line width is the resistance knob. Thixotropy is essential to the paste: it must flow under the squeegee and then stand without slumping, or the printed line blurs and the resistance drifts off value, and it comes from the shape of the glass frit particles.

children.name: Stainless steel mesh
children.description: The printing screen is a woven stainless-steel or nylon mesh stretched over a frame and photo-imaged. Stainless was standard because it must survive repeated abrasion by the abrasive paste in the paste.
children.note: Screen and stencil printing is documented for thick film. Not established: a woven stainless-steel or nylon mesh stretched over a frame and photo-imaged, and the abrasion argument. Note that the printed resistors are inside a sealed package, so the paste never meets the mesh in service.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.note: Screen and stencil printing is documented as the thick film deposition method. Not established: the photoemulsion-through-a-film exposure route, the 250-400 mesh, the 10-25 um wet film thickness, and the thixotropy-from-frit-particle-shape argument.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Tunnel-kiln firing of the printed bar
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A continuous belt or pusher kiln takes the printed substrate through a controlled temperature ramp so the resistors are 'aged' in the firing. Thick-film resistors are typically driven 50 percent above their rating for 15-25 minutes to burn in the grain boundaries and stabilise the value.

children.name: Continuous kiln
children.description: A belt or pusher kiln with profiled hot zones, carrying the printed bar through drying, burnout, peak and controlled cooling. The cooling rate matters as much as the peak, because too fast a cool micro-cracks the glass.
children.note: Firing at about 850 C is documented. Not established: the belt or pusher tunnel with profiled hot zones, the drying and burnout stages, and the claim that too fast a cool micro-cracks the glass.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: The 850 C firing peak is documented. Not established: driving the resistors at 1.5 times rated power for 15-25 minutes to age them in the firing, which is the substantive claim here.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Case, die and tension screw
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: The foil roll is sandwiched between a hardened case and a polished die with a slight bow. Turning the adjustment screw changes the roll's circumference, stretching the foil and raising the resistance by a controlled fraction of a part per million.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: The polished die was lapped on cast iron with progressively finer abrasive; a diamond paste finish gives sub-micron flatness.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Vacuum deposition bell
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Parts are racked in a vacuum chamber and the resistive film is deposited over the resistive area only, defined by a mask. The documented method for thin film resistors is sputtering; metal film resistors are usually nickel chromium, deposited by vacuum techniques of which sputtering is one. That vacuum deposition was standard for axial resistors in 1982 is reasonable but the exclusion of sputtering is not supported.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Contradicted as stated. The source says thin film resistors are made by sputtering, a method of vacuum deposition, and that metal film resistors are usually coated with nickel chromium by techniques that may include sputtering but need not be limited to it. Nothing supports 'vacuum deposited - not sputtered - was standard for axial resistors in 1982', nor the 50-500 nm film thickness or the 10^-3 to 10^-5 Torr figure.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon black furnace (soot reactor)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A refractory-lined combustion chamber with a ~1500 C flame and water-cooled steel scraper blades. Feed oil is sprayed across the flame; the resulting soot is scraped off as a mat and pelletised.

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.name: Capacitor wrap, sleeving and marking
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.description: Not a separate component but the packaging shared across the capacitor families: dipped epoxy for ceramic disc and monolithic parts, printed PVC or polyester sleeving for film caps, cardboard or aluminium sleeves for electrolytics, and printed value/brand markings on all of them.
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.note: The film and foil wrap is covered here for the ceramic and film parts, and under alu-electrolytic.assembly for the electrolytics.

children.name: E dipped conformal coat
children.description: Ceramic and monolithic parts were dip-coated in epoxy or PVC after firing to seal the porous body and to carry the printed marking. A dipped part looks identical to a moulded one, which is why it is hard to tell from a photograph whether a given C64 ceramic is disc or monolithic.

children.name: Dip-coating line
children.description: Parts on a wire rack are dipped in an epoxy or PVC solution and withdrawn so the coating tapers at both ends, leaving a characteristic tapered shoulder at the lead exit. A second dip gives the second shoulder.
children.note: Not established: wire-rack dipping, epoxy versus PVC solution as the coating, and the tapered-shoulder-at-each-lead-exit with a second dip giving the second shoulder.

children.name: Printed PVC sleeve
children.description: Film capacitors arrived in a printed plastic sleeve printed with the value, the rating and the maker. Sleeve polymer is the same PVC family as the case and the cable jacket.
children.note: Not established: a printed sleeve carrying value, rating and maker on the 250407 film capacitors, and PVC as the sleeve polymer.

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.name: Capacitor value marking ink
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.description: Values were printed on the sleeve or dipped coat in an oil-based or epoxy ink on an offset or screen coater. The two-digit and three-digit codes (104 for 100 nF, 104K5V) only became an industry standard in the 1970s.

mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.name: Vacuum-deposited counter-electrodes
mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.description: Aluminium or silver is evaporated or sputtered through a shadow-mask onto the mica sheets; sheets are stacked with a thin metallised layer between each, bonded under heat and pressure, and the stack is diced into individual capacitors.
mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.note: Vacuum evaporation was the 1982 technique; reactive sputtering of a dielectric was the later MIM form.

facts.label: Deposition
facts.value: vacuum evaporation or sputtering through a shadow mask

children.name: Aluminium electrode evaporation
children.description: Aluminium is evaporated rather than sputtered because it is cheap and vapourises at a manageable temperature; it is then left unoxidised under vacuum. Silver electrodes were used where the highest capacitance per unit area was needed.
children.note: Not established: that aluminium rather than silver was evaporated for the C64's mica capacitors, the manageability argument, and the silver electrodes used where maximum capacitance per unit area was needed. No source consulted describes mica capacitor electrode metallisation.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.name: Screen-printing internal electrodes
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.description: A metal paste is printed onto the green sheets to define the buried internal electrodes, the sheets being cut from the rolled foil afterwards. In 1982 the commodity MLCC still used a noble-metal paste: the displacement of palladium-bearing electrodes by cheaper nickel is dated to 1993 by TDK, with copper and nickel arriving later still after a late-1990s surge in noble-metal prices. So the older, expensive palladium-silver electrode was the mainstream choice at this date, not a legacy one.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.note: Not established, and in tension with the source cited: the switch from palladium-bearing to nickel internal electrodes is dated there to 1993 by TDK, with cheaper base metals developing after a late-1990s noble-metal price surge, not to the 1982 commodity part. Screen-printing a metal paste onto the green sheets is documented; the 1982 nickel-versus-palladium-silver balance is not.

facts.label: 1982 internal electrode
facts.value: palladium-silver or similar noble metal for a 1982 part; nickel only from 1993 and later base metals after that

facts.label: Print
facts.value: screen through a photoemulsion mask, offset on high-volume lines

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.name: Dicing into blanks
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.description: The laminated bar is cut with a resin-bonded diamond saw into hundreds or thousands of identical blanks, each one capacitor body. One sintered bar yields thousands of capacitors and one furnace run yields many bars, so the economics only work at that scale - which is why MLCC production had consolidated into a handful of very large Japanese, European and later Taiwanese plants by the early 1980s.

children.name: Resin-bonded diamond blade
children.description: A thin, flat, run-of-the-mill diamond wheel; the same abrasive technology as the crystal grinder but applied to a sintered ceramic bar.
children.note: Cutting the pressed stack into individual components is documented. Not established: that a resin-bonded diamond blade is used, or that this is 'the same abrasive technology as the crystal grinder'.
